title: Chapter 49: Lilies, Part 3 of 5: Lady Ashcombe
html:
But on the way to the stairs, somebody stopped her.
Not with a word. With a stick. A black stick, with a silver ferrule, held out across her path at the height of her knee, the way a gate comes down across a road. Lyra stopped, because otherwise she would have walked into it.
She looked down.
Old Lady Ashcombe was sitting in her chair by the wall of the hall, in black, very upright, with her little dog in her lap and her stick held out across the white marble in one thin hand. The hand was steady. The stick did not shake at all.
"Thorne," said Lady Ashcombe.
Her voice was high and thin and dry, like a dead leaf blowing across a step.
Lyra stood still.
The Duke had stopped too, a pace behind her. Lyra felt him stop. She felt him not say anything.
Lady Ashcombe looked up at her. She had small black eyes, very bright, sunk deep in a face so old and so lined that it looked like a walnut. She wore a black lace cap on her white hair, and jet at her throat, and her little dog was white and very fat and looked at Lyra out of the black lap with exactly the same small bright black eyes.
"I turned my back on you," said Lady Ashcombe. "On Saturday. At Ansel's."
"Yes."
"I meant to. I'm too old to do anything I don't mean to." The black eyes did not move from Lyra's face. "I thought you'd come in your mother's gown to beg. Thornes don't beg. Your grandfather would have starved in the street first. I thought you'd come to beg, and I was ashamed for her."
Lyra did not say anything.
"And now you've come to Cressida's," said Lady Ashcombe, "in the same gown. On the night after the woman who made it was killed. With your hair cut off. And your chin up." She lowered the stick. Slowly. Until its silver ferrule rested on the white marble between them. "That's not begging."
"No."
"What is it, then?"
Lyra thought about it.
"Rent," she said.
Lady Ashcombe's small black eyes looked at her for a long time.
Then something happened in the walnut face. A crack in it, at one corner of the thin mouth. Lyra did not know what it was at first. She had never seen it before. Nobody on the Hill had, perhaps, for years.
It was a smile.
"Rent," said Lady Ashcombe. "Yes. That's it. That's exactly it." She stroked the little white dog. "Sit down, girl. There. On the stool. For one minute. Ansel can spare you for one minute. Cressida's kept everybody else waiting for thirty years, she can wait for you."
There was a stool beside her chair. A little low footstool covered in white silk. Lyra sat down on it, in the gray gown, so that her face was lower than the old woman's. The Duke stood behind her, a great soft dark shape, and looked at the ceiling.
Lady Ashcombe leaned forward.
She smelled of camphor, and old lace, and something sharp and clean underneath, like lavender water. Not lilies. Lyra breathed it in and was grateful.
"I danced with your mother," said Lady Ashcombe. "At my own ball. The one she wore that gown to. Not danced. Walked. Round the room, arm in arm, the way old women and young women walk at a ball when the old woman is the hostess and the young woman is the only person in the room worth talking to." Her black eyes were very bright. "She asked me a question. That night. While we walked. She said, Lady Ashcombe, your husband had ships. Do you still know any captains who go east? Across the Narrow Sea? In winter?"
Lyra did not move.
"I said, Isolde, nobody goes east across the Narrow Sea in winter but smugglers and fools. And she laughed and said, Then give me the name of the best smuggler you know." Lady Ashcombe stroked the dog. "And I did. Saints help me. I thought it was a joke. I thought it was one of her jokes. She had a great many." She was quiet for a moment. "A month later she went to the coast. For her chest. And three months after that they buried an empty box at Saint Clement's with the lid nailed down, and I stood at the back of the church and thought about the name I'd given her. And never said a word. To anyone. In eleven years."
The sea roared in the shell of the hall. Somebody laughed by the urns.
"Why are you telling me?" said Lyra.
"Because I'm eighty-three," said Lady Ashcombe, "and I won't see another Midwinter. Dr. Quarles says so, and Dr. Quarles is a fool about most things but not about that." Her thin hand closed on the silver head of her stick. "And because you came to this house in her gown with your chin up, and paid your rent, and I'd like somebody to know the name before I take it with me."
She bent forward, closer, until her thin dry lips were nearly at Lyra's ear, and her camphor smell was all Lyra could breathe.
"Fey," she said. "Captain Fey. Of the Lantern. That was the name I gave her. It was the father, then. It'll be the daughter now, if she's still flying."
She sat back.
And lifted her stick off the marble, and laid it across her knees again, over the little dog, and looked away across the hall at the urns, at the lilies, at nothing. As if Lyra were not there at all. As if the stool were empty.
"Go on," she said. "Cressida's waiting. Don't drink from the cups."
Lyra stood up.
She stood for a moment beside the old woman's chair, in the gray gown, looking down at the black lace cap and the walnut face and the small bright black eyes that would not look at her.
Then she bent down, quickly, and kissed the old woman's cheek. It was dry and soft and cold, like a leaf.
Lady Ashcombe did not move.
But her thin hand, on the little white dog, went still. And stayed still. And Lyra, straightening up, saw the small black eyes, looking away across the hall at nothing, go suddenly very bright, and wet.
"Go on," said Lady Ashcombe again. Not dry. Not thin. "Go on, child. Before I make a fool of myself in Cressida Thorne's hall."
Lyra went.
The Duke of Marrow walked her to the foot of the lily stairs. He did not say anything about Lady Ashcombe. He did not say anything at all. But at the bottom step, where the footman in white was waiting to take her up, he stopped, and looked down at her, and his sleepy gray-green eyes were not sleepy.
"Fey," he said, very low. "I'd forgotten that name. I'd put it away." He let go of her arm. "Go up. And come down again. I'll be here."
The White Room
The footman took her up the stairs.
Not the Duke. The Duke stayed below, on his white silk sofa by the door of the long room, with his cane across his knees and his eyes half shut, and let her go. He did not say anything. He only lifted one ringed hand off the gold head of the cane, a little, as she went. The way you lift a hand to somebody going out to sea.
Up the white stairs. Between the ropes of lilies. Their heavy heads brushed her shoulders as she passed, and left gold pollen on the gray silk, and she did not brush it off. Up to the gallery at the top, where the two white arms of the staircase met. Along a corridor, carpeted in white, so thick that her mother's slippers made no sound. Past white doors, shut. To a white door at the end, standing a little open, with warm light coming out round its edge.
The footman opened it for her, and stood aside, and looked at the air above her head.
She went in.
It was the same room. She had known it would be. She had been here once before, in the autumn, with Corin behind her in a borrowed green footman's coat with a silver rod in its long pocket and his face as still as stone. She had sat in this room with her mother's cup in her hands and listened to her aunt tell her she was so like her, so terribly like her.
White. Everything white. A small square room, warm, close, with a fire in a little white marble grate. White walls. White silk curtains drawn across the window. A thick white carpet. Two white velvet chairs by the fire, facing each other. Between them a low round table with a white cloth edged in white lace, and on the cloth a tray, and on the tray a silver teapot, and a silver jug of cream, and a silver bowl of sugar. And two cups.
Small. Thin. White. So thin that the firelight came through them. Eggshell china, with a band of silver round the rim.
And against the far wall, beside the fire, the cabinet. Tall. Pale wood, painted white, gilded at the edges. Two glass doors. Seven shelves behind the glass, lined with blue velvet. And on the shelves, in rows, things. Small things. Each on its own square of velvet, with space round it, the way jewelers lay out their best rings.
She did not look at the cabinet. Not yet.
Cressida was sitting in one of the white chairs.
She had taken off her long white gloves. They lay folded in her white lap. Her hands were bare. Long and white and fine, with no rings at all. She was pouring the tea. She did it slowly, beautifully, the way she did everything, with the silver pot held high, so that the tea went down into the first thin white cup in a long gold thread, and steamed.
And as the tea rose in the cup, something came up through it. Out of the bottom. Small, and silver, and shining.
A mask. A tiny silver mask, in the bottom of the cup, with two tiny eye holes. Blinking up at the ceiling through the gold of the tea.
"Sit down, darling," said Cressida, without looking up. "Your tea's poured."
Lyra sat down in the other white chair.
Cressida filled the second cup. The second mask came up blinking through the gold. She set down the pot. She took a small pair of silver tongs and dropped two lumps of sugar into Lyra's cup, one, two, without asking, the way she had done in the autumn. And a little cream. And stirred it, with a small silver spoon, round and round, so that the mask in the bottom seemed to turn and look, and turn and look.
Then she held it out.
Lyra took it.
She held it in both her gloved hands, the way she had held it in the autumn. Madame Hesper's gloves round her mother's cup. It was very hot. The heat came through the old kid into her palms. She looked down into it. At the tea, pale gold with cream. At the little silver mask in the bottom, looking up at her.
A cup that has a mask in the bottom, my dear, is a cup that is watching you while you drink.
She did not drink.
She held it, and did not lift it, and looked at her aunt over it.
Cressida was watching her. Over her own cup. With the Thorne eyes. Gray, and clear, and a little long at the corners. And after a moment, the red mouth smiled.
"Ansel told you not to drink it," she said.
Lyra did not answer.
"Of course he did. He always does. He tells everyone." Cressida lifted her own cup and drank from it. A small neat sip. She set it down on its saucer. "Ansel has a great many ideas about my cups. He's never once been brave enough to find out if any of them are true." She folded her bare hands on the gloves in her lap. "It's only tea, darling. With a little cream. Your mother brought them from Marrowmere, and I use them because they're beautiful, and because they were hers, and because it makes me feel close to her." Her eyes went bright. "Is that so very wicked?"
Lyra held the cup and did not drink.
Cressida watched her not drink it for a long moment.
Then she laughed. The small soft shaken laugh.
"Oh, you are like her," she said. "You are. She never drank from them either. Not once. In all the years." She shook her head, and the white glass beads on the ends of the long pins in her hair flashed and went dark. "Well. Hold it, then. Hold it and get warm. You look frozen, darling. You've been out in the snow a great deal this week, I think."
The fire ticked in the little white grate.
"And how is your harvester?" said Cressida.
She said it lightly. Pleasantly. As if she were asking after a dog that Lyra used to have.
Lyra had been waiting for it. The Duke had told her. Whatever you say to that, she will believe the opposite. So decide before you get there what you want her to believe.
She had decided in the carriage. On the long climb up the Hill, with the Duke asleep across from her and the gas lamps going past the window one after another.
She would tell the truth.
"He's dying," she said.
Cressida's cup stopped. Just for a moment. Halfway to her red mouth. Then went on.
"The Ash is past his elbows," said Lyra. Her voice was very steady. "Gray. Both arms. His fingers don't feel the pencil any more. He's burned his first language and the night he came to Tallow Street and three winters and a word for his mother, and he can't count past nine. A rod went into the back of his leg on Saturday at the Bridewell, and on Tuesday he walked on it anyway, and now the knee won't bend. It never will. He can't walk without somebody holding him up." She looked at her aunt over the cup. "He's lying on a bench in the dark tonight, Aunt Cressida, with a book on his chest. He reads the first page of it every morning so that he remembers his own name. One day soon he'll read it and it won't help."
The fire ticked.
Cressida Thorne looked at her niece across the little white table for a long time.
And Lyra watched her face. Watched the long fine pale face with the red mouth and the Thorne eyes. And saw, very clearly, the way you see a fish move under clear water, her aunt not believe a word of it.
Saw her think: She's lying. He's strong. He's well. He's on his feet somewhere, close, and she's covering for him.
And saw her, a moment after that, look away. At the fire. And her bare white hand went to her throat. To the three ropes of pearls. And rested there.
"Poor man," said Cressida softly. "Poor, poor man." She took her hand away from her pearls. "You must be so tired, darling. Looking after him. And your father. And all your little friends in the snow." She smiled. "Drink your tea."
Lyra did not drink her tea.
She put the cup down on its saucer, on the white lace cloth, very carefully, so that it did not clink. The little silver mask in the bottom looked up at the ceiling.
Then she folded her gloved hands in her gray silk lap, and looked at her aunt, and said:
"Aunt Cressida. Who pays my father's nurse?"
The Nurse
Cressida did not answer at once.
She sat in her white velvet chair with her bare hands folded on the long white gloves in her lap, and looked at her niece across the little table, and her face did not change at all. It stayed exactly as it had been. Soft. Sorrowful. Fond. As if Lyra had asked her what time it was.
Then she picked up her cup, and drank from it, and put it down.
"I do, darling," she said.
Just like that.
"Her name is Mrs. Fell," said Cressida. "Agatha Fell. A widow. Very respectable. She was a nurse in the war, at a field hospital in the north, and afterward at the Ministry's house for officers at Fallowfield. When your father was taken there, she asked for him particularly. She said she'd known him, a long time ago. When he was young." Cressida turned her cup a little on its saucer. "Fallowfield is a charity house, Lyra. It pays its nurses very badly. So I pay her a little more. Every month. To be sure that she stays. To be sure that he's comfortable. That he's warm, and fed, and kept clean, and turned in his bed at night." She looked up. "Is that so very wicked, too?"
Lyra did not move.
"And to write in his notes," she said, "patient taps."
The fire ticked.
"Every day for two years," said Lyra. "Nothing else. Not patient tapped four times and then two. Not patient tapped the same numbers over and over and then stopped, as if waiting. Not patient answered when a sergeant tapped back. Just patient taps. As if it was a cough." Her voice did not shake. "Did you pay her for that too, Aunt Cressida? To write it like that? So that nobody who read the notes would ever think to listen?"
Cressida looked at her for a long time.
Then she set her cup down on its saucer, very carefully, so that it did not clink. And leaned back in her white velvet chair. And for the first time since she had come down the lily stairs, something in her long fine face changed.
It was not much. It was only that the sorrow went out of it. And the fondness. And what was left underneath them was very still, and very tired, and older than Lyra had ever seen it.
"Yes," said Cressida Thorne.
Lyra had known. She had known since Corin said it, in the crypt, with his gray hand on the Ledger. Sundries, Fallowfield, monthly, by the Councillor's hand. She had known on the long climb up the Hill. She had known on the stairs, between the lilies.
It was still like being hit.
"Why?"
Cressida looked at the fire.
"Because a man who taps is a man who is still trying to say something," she said. "And there were people, darling, who would have been very interested in what your father was trying to say. And who would have come to Fallowfield to listen. And who, when they had heard it, would have made very sure that he never tapped again." She turned her gray eyes back to Lyra. "I paid Agatha Fell to write patient taps, and nothing else, every day, for two years, so that every clerk and every doctor and every Inquisitor who ever read his notes would think what you thought, before you knew. That it was a cough. A wheel, still going round. Nothing." She paused. "So that he would be left alone."
The fire ticked.
"I kept him alive," said Cressida. "Do you understand? For two years. With a widow's wages and a dull line in a ledger. While you were writing your fierce little letters to your brother and stealing back your mother's things out of the pawnshops on Silk Street. I kept your father alive by making sure that nobody ever listened to him."
Lyra sat in the white chair with her hands in her lap.
She thought of a sergeant with a bad leg sitting at a long table on a barge, tapping back on her father's hand. And her father looking at him, properly, with his eyes. Drum. Drummer. The drummer. Find—
She thought of Silas Kross, at his green leather desk, every day, for two years. Tapping. And waiting.
"Who?" she said. "Who would have come to listen?"
Cressida smiled.
It was not the red smile of the stairs. It was smaller, and thinner, and it did not reach her eyes at all.
"You know who, darling," she said. "You've seen him tonight. Standing by my fire, listening to my music, tapping on my glass." She picked up her cup again. "He's been tapping it for two years. Hoping somebody, somewhere, would answer. And nobody has." She drank. "Except, I hear, a Watch sergeant on Monday. Under a table. Once."
Lyra went cold.
All the way through. From the top of her head to the soles of her mother's slippers.
"How do you know that?"
"Because I'm a Councillor of this city," said Cressida, "and I make it my business to know what the Inquisitor of the Office has for breakfast." She set her cup down. "And because he told me. Tonight. By the fire. Before you came. He was so pleased about it, Lyra. You can't imagine. He said it was the first answer in two years. He said he was going to have the sergeant back on Thursday next and hold his hand."
The fire ticked in the little white grate.
And Lyra understood, sitting there in her mother's gown in her aunt's white room, that she had been wrong about something. She did not know yet what. Only that the room had tilted, very slightly, under her, the way the floor of the crypt had tilted when she read St Bride's on her brother's letter.
"You're afraid of him," she said slowly.
Cressida did not answer.
"The Duke said. He's the only guest on the Hill you're afraid of. And you ask him every year."
"Of course I ask him." Cressida's voice was very soft. "A woman who is afraid of a dog, darling, does not lock it out of the garden. She feeds it. On her own lawn. Where she can see it." She looked at Lyra. "Every year I give Silas Kross a glass of my wine and a chair by my fire and the best music on the Hill, and I watch him tap. And every year he watches me. And every year he goes home, and nothing happens." She paused. "That is what keeping someone alive looks like, on the Hill. It isn't brave. It isn't pretty. It's tea, and wine, and a widow's wages, and a dull line in a ledger."
Lyra sat very still.
She did not know if it was true.
That was the worst of it. She sat in the white room and looked at her aunt and did not know if any of it was true. Any of it at all. It sounded true. It sounded like the truest thing anybody had ever said to her. And her aunt's face, with the sorrow gone out of it, looked like the face of somebody telling the truth.
Whatever you say, the Duke had said, she will believe the opposite.
He had not said what to do when it was the other way round.
